events.title: Canada, US 'Far Apart' in Trade Talks Four Days Before 50% Section 338 Tariffs Hit $20B of Canadian Goods
events.detail: Canadian Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc told a government advisory group Saturday that Canada and the US remain significantly divided in talks meant to head off a fresh round of 50% Section 338 tariffs — covering roughly $20 billion of Canadian autos, alcohol, and dairy exports, including USMCA-qualifying goods — set to take effect at 12:01am EDT Wednesday, August 19. LeBlanc has met US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer four times in three weeks (most recently Thursday, August 13), with talks continuing through the weekend; sticking points include Canada's 25% retaliatory tariff on US vehicles, provincial restrictions on American alcohol sales, and dairy quota arrangements, while Canada is separately pushing for relief from existing US steel and aluminum tariffs. Canadian Chamber of Commerce CEO Candace Laing said both sides are exploring an interim agreement that would bundle the new threat together with tariffs already in place. The standoff is the latest flashpoint in the broader 2026 tariff cycle — alongside the July 24 Section 122/Section 301 transition — that continues to weigh on the US effective tariff rate and cross-border trade volumes.

events.title: Section 122 Tariff Surcharge Expires by Statute; Section 301 Forced-Labor Tariffs (10-12.5%) on 60 Economies Take Effect Same Minute
events.detail: The Section 122 emergency tariff surcharge expired by operation of law at 12:01 a.m. EDT on July 24, 2026 — 150 days after its February 24 effective date, the statutory maximum without an Act of Congress, which did not occur. In its place, USTR's final action in its forced-labor Section 301 investigations took effect the same minute, imposing 10% or 12.5% ad valorem tariffs on goods from 60 trading-partner economies found to have inadequately enforced bans on forced-labor imports, including a 12.5% tier on Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Canada, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, Mexico, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago, and the UK. Goods from Canada and Mexico entered duty-free under USMCA, and CAFTA-DR textile/apparel goods, are exempt, as are goods already in transit before July 24 if entered by July 28. The transition avoided the tariff-revenue coverage gap that trade counsel had flagged as a risk going into the cliff, since the Section 301 final rule was published and made operative in time.

kpis.deltaNote: MAY 2026 (released June 25): Headline PCE 4.1% YoY (+0.4% MoM) — highest since April 2023. Core PCE 3.4% YoY (vs 3.3% forecast). Personal income and spending each +0.7% MoM; saving rate held at 3%. Released just over a week after Warsh's hawkish dot plot, complicating the disinflation narrative even as Iran-deal oil relief began working through the data. June CPI (July 14) subsequently cooled to 3.5%, suggesting May PCE may mark the cycle high.

kpis.label: Fed Funds Rate
kpis.source: Federal Reserve FOMC, July 29 2026 (held; 3 hawkish dissents)
kpis.delta: Held at 3.50-3.75%; 3 dissents wanted a hike
kpis.deltaNote: July 28-29: FOMC held at 3.50-3.75% despite the July 23 oil-driven inflation scare that had pushed September hike odds to ~82%. Three members dissented in favor of a hike — Warsh called it a 'good family fight.' The Aug 7 jobs miss (NFP -23K) subsequently cooled hike expectations for September.

kpis.label: ECB Deposit Facility Rate
kpis.source: ECB Governing Council, June 11 2026 (25bp hike — first since July 2023)
kpis.deltaNote: June 11: ECB raised all three key rates 25bp — deposit facility to 2.25%, main refi to 2.40%, marginal lending to 2.65% (effective June 17). First hike since July 2023, reversing the final step of the prior 8-cut easing cycle. New staff projections: HICP 3.0% (2026)/2.3% (2027)/2.0% (2028); growth cut to 0.8%/1.2%/1.5%. Lagarde left the door open to further tightening.

kpis.label: US 10Y / 30Y Treasury Yield
kpis.value: 10Y ~4.65% (Aug 13) — Eased Further on Flat PPI; Hormuz Tanker Attack Aug 14 Renews Upside Risk
kpis.source: CNBC / Federal Reserve H.15 / FRED; July 23 - August 14, 2026
kpis.delta: Round-tripped a full cycle: surged on the July 23 Hormuz/Red Sea oil shock, fell back after the Aug 7 jobs miss, then eased a further ~4bp to 4.65% on Aug 13's flat PPI — before the Aug 14 UAE tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz reintroduced energy-shock upside risk.

The Aug 7 jobs report and Aug 13 flat PPI (below the 0.2% forecast) both reversed hike repricing, pulling September hike odds under 35% and the 10Y down to 4.65%. The Aug 14 attack on two UAE tankers in the Strait of Hormuz — the second in under a week — rebounded oil prices and re-injected energy-driven inflation risk just as soft retail sales and a crumbling Michigan sentiment reading pointed toward growth weakness instead.

kpis.label: US Consumer Confidence (CB Index)
kpis.delta: +0.3 from Apr 2026 revised (beat 91.9 forecast; first monthly decline vs revised level)
kpis.deltaNote: May 2026: CB 93.1 (beat ~91.9 forecast; released May 26) — Present Situation Index 121.2 (down 3.2 pts); Expectations Index 74.4 (16th consecutive month below 80 recession-warning threshold). Two-thirds of consumers cutting spending due to inflation (highest proportion outside official recession). Michigan Final May 44.8 (all-time record low in 70+ year survey history).

kpis.label: Michigan Consumer Sentiment (August 2026 Preliminary)
kpis.deltaNote: AUG 2026 PRELIMINARY (released Aug 14): 51.0, badly missing the 54.5 consensus and down from July's final 55.2. Index of Consumer Expectations fell more sharply than Current Conditions; short-term expectations -11%, long-term projections -17%. Only 8% of consumers expect income growth to outpace inflation. Year-ahead inflation expectations rose to 4.3%. Sentiment fell across demographic and political lines, sharpest among Republicans, older consumers, lower-income households, and those without college degrees. Still well above May 2026's all-time record low of 44.8, but the renewed slide — alongside July retail sales' steepest drop in over a year (Aug 14) — marks the clearest crack yet in the 'resilient consumer' narrative. Final August reading due Aug 28.

kpis.label: S&P 500 / Market Risk Gauge
kpis.value: S&P 500 Record Close 7,799 (Aug 13, +0.65%, First Close Above 7,800 Intraday); Slipped Aug 14 on Weak Retail Sales/Sentiment
kpis.source: CNBC / TheStreet / Federal Reserve; July 23 – August 14, 2026
kpis.delta: Sharp round trip and fresh record: the July 23 Hormuz/Red Sea oil shock knocked the Dow down 600+ points; markets recovered through the Jul 29 FOMC hold and Aug 7 jobs-driven rally, then set a fresh record 7,799 close on Aug 13's flat PPI before slipping fractionally Aug 14 on the retail-sales miss and Michigan sentiment plunge.
kpis.deltaNote: JULY 23-AUG 14 ARC: Oil-driven hike fears triggered the sharpest selloff of the window July 23. The FOMC's July 29 hold, the Aug 7 jobs shock, and Aug 12-13's cooling CPI/PPI prints drove a steady rally to a fresh S&P record (7,799, clearing 7,800 intraday) on Aug 13, with September hike odds falling under 35%. Aug 14 brought a pullback — retail sales fell 0.6% (steepest drop in over a year) and Michigan consumer sentiment tumbled to 51.0 — while a fresh Hormuz tanker attack rebounded oil prices, reintroducing energy-shock risk to the disinflation narrative.

kpis.label: US Avg Effective Tariff Rate
kpis.value: Section 301 Forced-Labor Tariffs (10-12.5%) on 60 Economies Live Since Jul 24; New Canada Section 338 Tariffs (50% on ~$20B) Loom Aug 19

kpis.contestNote: The Section 122 tariff surcharge expired by statute at 12:01am EDT July 24 (150 days after its Feb 24 effective date; no Congressional extension occurred). USTR's Section 301 forced-labor tariffs (10% or 12.5%, 60 economies) took effect the same minute, avoiding the tariff-revenue coverage gap that trade counsel had flagged as a risk in mid-July. Canada/Mexico USMCA-qualifying goods and CAFTA-DR textiles remain exempt from Section 301 — but a separate Section 338 threat targets Canada directly: 50% tariffs on ~$20B of autos, alcohol, and dairy (including USMCA-qualifying goods) are due to take effect Aug 19 absent a deal. Talks between USTR Greer and Canada's LeBlanc remained 'far apart' as of Aug 15, four meetings into three weeks of negotiation.

kpis.label: China GDP Q2 2026 (actual)
kpis.contestNote: Q2 2026 missed forecast (4.3% vs 4.5% expected), down from 5.0% in Q1 — slowest pace in roughly 3.5 years. H1 fixed-asset investment -5.7% YoY (real estate -18%). June activity data (Jul 15) was mixed: industrial production +5.3% YoY beat, retail sales +1.0% YoY soft. Stimulus speculation building ahead of the late-July Politburo meeting.
kpis.deltaNote: Q1 2026: 5.0% (front-loaded exports). Q2 2026: 4.3% — Iran war demand destruction and property-sector drag materializing as expected. IMF July WEO maintains global growth at 3.0% for 2026 but revised headline inflation up to 4.7%.

kpis.label: Global Policy Uncertainty / Recession Risk
kpis.value: AUG 14: July CPI (3.4%) and PPI (Flat) Both Cool, S&P Sets Record Above 7,800; Retail Sales -0.6% and Michigan Sentiment 51.0 Crack the Consumer Story; Hormuz Tanker Attack Renews Oil Risk

That disinflation narrative was complicated Aug 14: July retail sales fell 0.6%, the steepest monthly drop in over a year, and the University of Michigan's preliminary August sentiment reading tumbled to 51.0 (from July's 55.2), pulling stocks off their record highs. Next catalysts: the final August Michigan sentiment reading (Aug 28), August jobs and CPI reports, and the September 16-17 FOMC meeting.

kpis.source: Bank of Japan, June 16 2026 (25bp hike — highest since 1995)

The hike landed the same day Warsh's first FOMC opened, raising August-2024-style carry-unwind concerns; the immediate market reaction was orderly (Nikkei +0.46%), but the yen still fell to a fresh 40-year low past 162/USD by June 30 despite the hike and an estimated $72.5bn in prior FX intervention.

events.title: Day 682 — Peso Strengthens to 16.98/USD as Sheinbaum Confirms Tamaulipas Hospital Tour
events.detail: On August 14, 2026 (Day 682, Friday), Sheinbaum noted the peso trading at 16.98 per US dollar and said she expects H2 2026 growth to strengthen as previously delayed public works — held up mainly by bureaucratic bottlenecks — begin construction: 'Each month is going to be better.' She also confirmed a weekend work tour to Tamaulipas with Governor Américo Villarreal to inaugurate two new hospitals (ISSSTE and IMSS-Bienestar), review hydraulic works, and meet with 'Jóvenes Construyendo el Futuro' participants.

events.title: Day 681 — AMLO's Son Andy López Beltrán Says US Revoked His Visa, Adding Pressure on Sheinbaum
events.detail: On August 13, 2026 (Day 681, Thursday), Andrés Manuel 'Andy' López Beltrán — son of former president AMLO — announced via a letter posted to Instagram and addressed to Donald Trump that the U.S. State Department, under Secretary Marco Rubio and Deputy Secretary Christopher Landau, had revoked his U.S. visa. López Beltrán called the move 'political, more propagandistic than anything, in a Hitlerian style' and denied any wrongdoing. The episode increased scrutiny on the Sheinbaum government amid separate PAN questions linking López Beltrán to an FGR fuel-theft ('huachicol fiscal') investigation.

events.title: Day 680 — Sheinbaum Meets Goldman Sachs President Waldron to Discuss Plan México Investment
events.detail: On August 12, 2026 (Day 680, Wednesday), President Sheinbaum met at the National Palace with Goldman Sachs President and COO John E. Waldron, alongside Finance Secretary Edgar Amador Zamora, to discuss Mexico's 'favorable perception' among international investors and opportunities under Plan México, which targets 1.5 million new jobs and investment above 25% of GDP as Mexico aims to move from the world's 15th- to a top-10 economy. No specific investment agreements or new projects were disclosed following the meeting.

events.title: Day 676 — US Partially Resumes Avocado Inspections After Mexico Deploys 1,557 Troops to Michoacán
events.detail: On August 8, 2026 (Day 676, Saturday), the U.S. Embassy began a partial resumption of avocado export inspections in Michoacán, three days after the August 5 suspension, covering the municipalities of Tancítaro, Tacámbaro, Uruapan, and the Morelia–Pátzcuaro corridor. The restart followed a security agreement under which the Mexican government deployed 1,557 Army and National Guard personnel to the avocado belt on August 6 and established a permanent coordination table to monitor conditions protecting U.S. inspectors. The resumption remained partial and contingent on continued security improvements, with full normalization pending across the roughly 60 export packing plants in the state.

events.title: Day 674 — Sheinbaum Rules Out Fracking Expansion in Key Basin, Citing Water Tables and Indigenous Communities
events.detail: On August 6, 2026 (Day 674, Thursday), President Sheinbaum announced that her government would not expand fracking (hydraulic fracturing) operations in a key northern petroleum basin, citing risks to regional water tables and nearby Indigenous communities. The announcement marked a partial reversal from an earlier, more open stance in which Sheinbaum had floated the possibility of 'new extraction technologies' distinct from traditional fracking methods as a way to boost domestic natural gas and oil output amid declining Pemex production. The decision underscored the balancing act facing her administration between reducing Mexico's growing dependence on U.S. natural gas imports and honoring environmental and social commitments central to the Fourth Transformation platform. The move followed years of pressure from environmental and Indigenous rights groups opposed to fracking expansion in northern Mexico.

events.title: Day 674 — Sheinbaum's Approval Jumps to 57% as Inflation Cools to Near Six-Year Low
events.detail: On August 6, 2026 (Day 674, Thursday), Bloomberg News published new AtlasIntel LatAm Pulse polling showing President Sheinbaum's approval rating rising to 57%, an 8-point jump from the prior month's survey. The rebound followed a rocky summer stretch in which her approval had dipped below 50% for the first time in early July amid concerns over falling purchasing power and rising prices. Pollsters and analysts linked the improvement to two factors: annual headline inflation falling for four consecutive months — from 4.6% in March to 3.12% in July, the lowest level since May 2020 and back inside Banxico's target range — and Sheinbaum's increasingly vocal pushback against the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, including sharpened criticism of ICE following the July 7 killing of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston. The rebound reversed months of erosion in her approval that had been driven by the Q1 2026 GDP contraction, the CIA-Chihuahua sovereignty controversy, and broader economic anxiety.

events.title: Day 673 — US Suspends Avocado Export Inspections in Michoacán Over Threat to Inspectors
events.detail: On August 5, 2026 (Day 673, Wednesday), the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) halted phytosanitary inspections required for Mexican avocado exports in Michoacán, citing an unspecified 'threat against U.S. interests' after inspectors received threats in the field. The suspension immediately froze new certifications needed to ship avocados to the United States, Mexico's overwhelming top export market (roughly 90% of Mexican avocado exports by volume, worth $3.65 billion in 2025). Michoacán supplies 75-80% of Mexico's total avocado output and the industry directly employs over 200,000 people in the state. It marked the third U.S. suspension of Michoacán avocado inspections since 2022, all tied to security incidents against American inspectors. Michoacán Governor Alfredo Ramírez Bedolla said the pause was intended to safeguard inspectors following recent security incidents and extortion-related arrests in the region.

events.title: Day 667 — Q2 2026 GDP Grows 2.1% Annually, Strongest Quarterly Rebound Since Late 2020, Boosted by World Cup Spending
events.detail: On July 30, 2026 (Day 667, Thursday), INEGI released preliminary Q2 2026 GDP data showing the Mexican economy grew 2.1% year-on-year, a sharp rebound from the 0.4% annual expansion recorded in Q1 2026. On a seasonally adjusted quarter-on-quarter basis, GDP rose 1.5%, reversing Q1's 0.6% contraction and marking the strongest quarterly expansion since Q4 2020. All three broad sectors improved versus Q1: services rose 1.5% QoQ (from -0.4%), industry rose 1.6% QoQ (from -1.0%), and the primary sector jumped 3.3% QoQ (from -1.7%) on a sharp agricultural rebound. Analysts attributed part of the rebound to a surge in consumer and tourism spending tied to Mexico hosting 16 FIFA World Cup 2026 matches in June and July, alongside resilient domestic consumption. Economy officials said the results kept the government's 1.5% full-year 2026 growth target within reach provided the second half of the year did not see a renewed contraction, even as private-sector forecasters (OECD, Citi, IMF) maintained more cautious full-year estimates in the 0.8–1.6% range reflecting continued uncertainty from the unresolved USMCA review and U.S. tariff exposure.

events.title: Day 638 — USMCA Mandatory Six-Year Joint Review: US Declines to Extend Agreement, Triggering Annual Review Process
events.detail: On July 1, 2026 (Day 638), the USMCA Free Trade Commission held its mandatory six-year joint review under Article 34.7 of the trade agreement. Mexico and Canada had formally proposed renewing the agreement through 2042, but the United States declined to confirm its intention to extend USMCA for a new 16-year term, stating it 'did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form.' The decision does not terminate the agreement; instead it triggers an annual joint-review mechanism under Article 34.7.4 that will repeat each year until the three parties either agree to an extension or the agreement's ten-year sunset clock runs out, expiring July 1, 2036 absent action. Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard represented Mexico at a virtual trilateral meeting held the same day. President Sheinbaum had said in the run-up that her government was 'calm' because Mexico had fulfilled its obligations under the review process, and that the outcome 'depends a lot on the U.S. government's position' — reiterating that the agreement serves the interests of all three countries. She noted the treaty's underlying ten-year renewal architecture would require passage through each country's congress if a contrary U.S. position persisted. USTR Ambassador Jamieson Greer issued a separate statement on the U.S. position the same day. The outcome left North American trade relations in a state of managed uncertainty heading into the second half of 2026.

events.title: Day 628 — CNTE Teachers' Strike Ends After 20 Days; Union Returns to Classrooms Without Reversal of 2007 ISSSTE Pension Law
events.detail: On June 21, 2026 (Day 628, Saturday), the CNTE national teachers' union formally ended its 20-day national strike, which had shut down classrooms across 29 states, blockaded the Zócalo in Mexico City, and threatened disruptions of FIFA World Cup 2026 events including the June 11 opening match at Estadio Azteca. CNTE representative Pedro Hernández announced the end of the action, stating: 'Today, we are returning to our classrooms because we intend to honor our commitments to our students, their communities, and their parents.' The strike had centered on two core demands: a salary increase and reversal of the 2007 ISSSTE pension law, which the Sheinbaum government maintained was fiscally unfeasible to abrogate outright. The union ultimately returned to classes without securing repeal of the pension law, accepting instead the government's proposed dialogue framework (a working table, diagnostic period, and formal proposals process running through August 31) that SEGOB and SEP had offered earlier in June. President Sheinbaum had maintained throughout the standoff that her government would not respond to 'provocations' and would keep channels of dialogue open through SEP and Gobernación rather than negotiate directly. The strike's end came 10 days after the World Cup opener and removed a major domestic political flashpoint during the tournament's run in Mexico.

events.title: Day 614 — Mexico's Olinia Electric Vehicle Officially Unveiled: First Domestically Designed EV; Ceremonial World Cup Role June 11
events.detail: On June 7, 2026 (Day 614, Sunday), Mexico's first domestically designed and assembled electric mini-car — the Olinia — was officially unveiled ahead of the FIFA World Cup 2026. The name 'Olinia' derives from the Nahuatl word meaning 'to move.' The vehicle was developed under the Sheinbaum government's national industrial policy framework and backed by public investment through the Plan México nearshoring and domestic manufacturing agenda. The prototype comes in three versions: a cargo utility vehicle, a personal passenger car, and a taxi/shared-mobility version, priced between 90,000 and 150,000 pesos (approximately USD 4,400–7,400 at prevailing MXN/USD rates). Mass production of an initial 20,000 units per year is planned to begin at a domestic manufacturing facility in 2027. The Olinia was given a ceremonial public-facing role at the World Cup inauguration at Estadio Azteca (Estadio Banorte) on June 11 — a high-visibility moment deliberately selected to signal Mexico's industrial pivot toward domestic automotive manufacturing and align the Sheinbaum government's climate commitments with economic nationalism. The launch positions Mexico among the few Latin American nations with a domestically conceived and produced electric vehicle. The Olinia was first mentioned publicly at Sheinbaum's May 13, 2026 mañanera.

events.title: Day 614 — CNTE Strike Day 7: SEGOB Formally Exhorts Teachers to End Zócalo Sit-In After SEP-ISSSTE Proposals; CNTE Threatens Airport and Stadium Blockades at World Cup Opener
events.detail: On June 7, 2026 (Day 614, Sunday), Mexico's Interior Ministry (Gobernación/SEGOB) under Secretary Rosa Icela Rodríguez formally issued a public exhortation to the CNTE national teachers' union to conclude its Zócalo encampment and accept ongoing dialogue, following written proposals submitted by SEP (Education Ministry) and ISSSTE (federal employee pension institute). Gobernación described the government's proposals as 'serious, responsible, and within budgetary limits,' while signaling that the Sheinbaum administration's negotiating position remained unchanged: a legislatively guided process (working table by June 15, diagnostic period through July 20, proposals through mid-August, teacher consultation through August 31) rather than immediate abrogation of the 2007 ISSSTE pension law. The CNTE maintained its strike posture and announced it would consider further escalation measures targeting the Benito Juárez International Airport (AICM) and Estadio Azteca (Estadio Banorte) during the FIFA World Cup opening match — Mexico vs. South Africa, June 11. The strike's seventh consecutive day continued to affect over 2 million students across 29 states. President Sheinbaum remained on her weekend schedule and did not intervene directly in CNTE negotiations, maintaining her position that SEGOB and SEP are the designated government dialogue counterparts. The standoff entered its second week with both sides unmoved on core positions, and the international attention of the World Cup opening four days away creating acute political pressure on the government to resolve or manage the conflict before kickoff.

events.title: Day 613 — Sheinbaum Leads Jóvenes Construyendo el Futuro National Assembly in Xalapa, Veracruz; Program Reaches 3.5 Million Beneficiaries, 170B Pesos Since 2019
events.detail: On June 6, 2026 (Day 613, Saturday), President Claudia Sheinbaum led a national assembly of the Jóvenes Construyendo el Futuro (Youth Building the Future) federal labor-training program at the Kaná Museum in Xalapa, Veracruz, accompanied by Veracruz Governor Rocío Nahle García. Sheinbaum highlighted the program's cumulative achievements: 3.5 million beneficiaries served since 2019; a total public investment of over 170 billion pesos; each participant receives a monthly stipend, IMSS social security coverage, and one year of formal work experience with a private- or public-sector employer. She framed youth dignified employment as a constitutional right, not a privilege, drawing a contrast with previous administrations' zero-employment-for-youth policies. The program — the flagship youth development initiative inherited from the AMLO government and expanded under the 'Second Floor of the Fourth Transformation' — was presented as a concrete pillar of Sheinbaum's social investment agenda. Veracruz ranks among Mexico's highest concentrations of program beneficiaries. The event was notable as Sheinbaum's main public activity on the Saturday before the FIFA World Cup opener (June 11), signaling her focus on social program delivery over political optics.

events.title: Day 613 — CNTE Strike Day 6: Union Rejects Latest Pension Offer; Solidarity Forum with Ayotzinapa Families; Threatens World Cup Venue Blockades
events.detail: June 6, 2026 (Day 613) marked the sixth day of the CNTE national teachers' strike with no agreement reached. The union formally rejected the federal government's most recent pension proposal — which offered to strengthen PENSIONISSSTE and study the creation of a public insurance company — because it left the 2007 ISSSTE pension reform law intact, which is the CNTE's non-negotiable core demand. At least three protesters had been injured in earlier strike-related demonstrations. The CNTE organized a solidarity forum near the FIFA World Cup Fan Fest zone on Paseo de la Reforma, inviting the families of the 43 Ayotzinapa disappeared students and allied social movements to broaden its political coalition and increase international visibility. The union explicitly escalated its threat posture: it announced potential blockades of Mexico City's Benito Juárez International Airport (AICM) and Estadio Azteca (Estadio Banorte) during the FIFA World Cup opener (Mexico vs. South Africa, June 11) — with the slogan 'Si no hay solución, el balón no rodará' ('If there's no solution, the ball won't roll'). Interior Minister (SEGOB) Rosa Icela Rodríguez formally exhorted the CNTE on June 6 to accept the SEP and ISSSTE proposals and end its Zócalo encampment. The strike continued to affect over 2 million students across 29 states. With no direct presidential intervention authorized, the government remained exposed to the risk of the crisis intersecting with the World Cup's global media attention.

events.title: Day 612 — Sheinbaum Holds Mañanera from Minatitlán, Veracruz; Launches 93-Billion-Peso Petrochemical and Fertilizer Investment Plan 2026–2030
events.detail: On June 5, 2026 (Day 612), President Claudia Sheinbaum held her morning press conference from Minatitlán, Veracruz — one of Mexico's historically significant petrochemical hubs — where she launched a strategic investment plan for the petrochemical and fertilizer sector. The plan commits 93 billion pesos in public and mixed (public-private) investment over 2026–2030, aimed at strengthening Pemex's downstream productive capacity and reducing Mexico's dependence on imported petrochemicals and fertilizers. The announcement aligned strategically with the Pemex-Petrobras collaboration agreement announced at the June 2 mañanera, which focuses on deepwater exploration and mature field optimization. Key elements of the plan: expansion of existing petrochemical complexes at Minatitlán and Cosoleacaque; new fertilizer production capacity at the Pajaritos complex; private-sector participation through public-private partnership frameworks under Plan México. Sheinbaum also confirmed at the mañanera that Iran's national soccer team had arrived in Mexico on June 5, settling in Tijuana as their base camp ahead of the FIFA World Cup 2026. Profeco (consumer protection agency) simultaneously launched the 'Who's Who in the World Cup' (Quién es Quién en los Precios del Mundial) price monitoring operation covering approximately 274,000 products across Mexico City, Guadalajara, and Monterrey, to detect and sanction price gouging ahead of the tournament.

events.title: Day 612 — CNTE Strike Day 5: Latin Times Reports 'World Cup Shadow' as Talks Stall; Mexico Opens vs. South Africa June 11
events.detail: June 5, 2026 (Day 612) marked the fifth day of the CNTE national teachers' strike, with no agreement in sight. Latin Times published an analysis titled 'World Cup Shadow: Mexico's Teachers' Union Strike Escalates Days Before Kickoff,' noting the unique political tension of a labor crisis playing out in the shadow of FIFA World Cup 2026 — with Mexico playing South Africa in the tournament opener at Estadio Azteca just 6 days away on June 11. The CNTE encampment in Mexico City's Historic Center remained in place, affecting Fan Fest infrastructure access near the Zócalo. The strike continued affecting over 2 million students across 29 states. The government had not budged from its position: SEGOB (Rosa Icela Rodríguez) and SEP (Mario Delgado) remained the designated dialogue counterparts; President Sheinbaum had declined to meet directly with CNTE leadership. The CNTE had threatened to escalate actions to coincide with international World Cup coverage but had not yet specified the form. Al Jazeera separately reported on the unusual confluence of the FIFA World Cup 2026 and Mexico's unresolved labor dispute, providing international visibility to the CNTE's cause.

events.title: Day 611 — Sheinbaum Signs National Tomato Price Agreement with Producers and Distributors
events.detail: On June 4, 2026 (Day 611), President Claudia Sheinbaum presided over the signing of the 'National Agreement for the Ordering of Production, Supply, Commercialization and Fair Price of Tomato' (Acuerdo Nacional para el Ordenamiento de la Producción, Abasto, Comercialización y Precio Justo del Jitomate). The signing ceremony was relocated from the National Palace to the Ministry of Economy (Secretaría de Economía) building due to ongoing CNTE blockades in the Historic Center. The agreement was signed with agricultural producers, central market (Central de Abasto) representatives, and major supermarket chains. The government cited three structural causes for the three-month tomato price spike: (1) Frost damage to production zones in Florida (U.S.); (2) a crop disease outbreak in Sinaloa, Mexico's top tomato-producing state; (3) excessive intermediary markups in the supply chain — 'coyotes' buying cheaply from producers and selling at inflated prices to retailers. The agreement creates direct connections between producers and central market distribution, bypassing traditional intermediary layers. Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard and Agriculture Secretary Columba Jasmin López participated. Sheinbaum had announced the June 4 signing date at her June 1 mañanera (it was originally announced for June 3 but delayed one day). The tomato crisis had become emblematic of food affordability concerns ahead of the FIFA World Cup 2026, with millions of tourists expected in Mexico City, Guadalajara, and Monterrey from June 11.

events.title: Day 611 — Sheinbaum Defends Ex-President AMLO's Letter to Trump at Mañanera; CNTE Enters Day 4 Without Agreement
events.detail: At her June 4, 2026 (Day 611) mañanera, President Claudia Sheinbaum defended and projected on screen a letter published by former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador (AMLO) that warned against foreign interference in Mexico and questioned the role of U.S. officials in domestic affairs. Sheinbaum thanked AMLO for his 'support' and accused the U.S. Republican far-right of attempting to use Mexico as a political weapon ahead of U.S. November 2026 midterm elections and the 2027 presidential race. The public endorsement of AMLO's letter represented a notable alignment between the ex-president and his successor, reinforcing the sovereignty narrative that has dominated the Sheinbaum administration since the CIA-Chihuahua affair in May. The mañanera also addressed the ongoing CNTE teachers' strike: Day 4 ended without any agreement between CNTE leadership and SEGOB. CNTE reiterated its demand for a direct meeting with Sheinbaum as a precondition for progress. Sheinbaum again declined, stating 'No vamos a reprimir' (We will not repress) while maintaining that negotiations must proceed through SEP and SEGOB channels. Affected students now exceeded 2 million across 29 states. The World Cup opening match — Mexico vs. South Africa at Estadio Azteca — was 7 days away.

events.title: Senate Confirms Brett Matsumoto as BLS Commissioner, Ending Year-Long Vacancy
events.detail: The Senate confirmed career economist Brett Matsumoto as commissioner of the Bureau of Labor Statistics on August 7, 2026, in a 51-47 vote covering a block of nominees. The role had been vacant since President Trump abruptly fired commissioner Erika McEntarfer in August 2025 over a weak July 2025 jobs report, and after Trump's initial pick, Heritage Foundation economist E.J. Antoni, was withdrawn amid Republican opposition. Matsumoto, who holds a Ph.D. in economics from UNC Chapel Hill, joined BLS in 2015 as an inflation expert and was on leave at the White House Council of Economic Advisers when selected. He will serve a four-year term overseeing US jobs and inflation data.

events.title: USTR Finalizes Section 301 Forced-Labor Tariffs on Over 80 Trading Partners
events.detail: The Office of the US Trade Representative finalized a broad Section 301 tariff action on July 23, 2026 covering more than 80 trading partners, taxing imports at 10% or 12.5% depending on the country's enforcement record on forced-labor import bans. The new duties, which took effect at midnight, replaced Trump's temporary 10% global Section 122 tariff that expired the same day. Trading partners facing the baseline 10% rate include Canada, Mexico, India, and the United Kingdom. The action followed a public comment period that closed July 6 and hearings held July 7.

events.title: Trump Escalates Trade War: 50% Tariffs on Canada, Forced-Labor Tariffs on 80+ Countries Take Effect
events.detail: Trump announced new 50% Section 338 tariffs on Canadian dairy, alcohol, furniture, and motor vehicles on July 20, 2026, effective August 19 — covering roughly $16-20 billion in annual imports. Three days later, on July 23, the USTR finalized a separate Section 301 forced-labor tariff action covering more than 80 trading partners (10-12.5% depending on enforcement record), replacing the temporary 10% Section 122 global tariff that expired the same day. Partners including Canada, Mexico, India, and the UK now face the new baseline 10% rate on top of sector-specific duties. Analysts called the moves a warning shot ahead of further trade actions.

events.title: Trump Announces 50% Tariffs on Canadian Dairy, Alcohol, Vehicles Under Section 338
events.detail: President Trump announced on July 20, 2026 that his administration will impose additional 50% ad valorem tariffs on a range of Canadian products — dairy, alcoholic beverages, furniture, and motor vehicles — under Section 338 of the Tariff Act, effective 12:01 a.m. ET on August 19, 2026. The move came via three separate proclamations alleging Canadian discrimination against US commerce in those sectors. USTR estimated the tariffs affect nearly $20 billion in annual Canadian imports (reported elsewhere as up to $16 billion for the targeted categories). Analysts described the move as a warning shot to other trading partners ahead of pending Section 301 forced-labor tariff decisions.

events.title: USTR Finalizes 25% Section 301 Tariff on Brazil, Effective July 22
events.detail: The Office of the US Trade Representative finalized a Notice of Action on July 15, 2026 imposing an additional 25% Section 301 tariff on a broad range of Brazilian-origin goods, effective for goods entered for consumption on or after July 22, 2026. The action followed a Section 301 investigation opened in July 2025 into Brazilian trade practices including digital-trade and electronic-payment restrictions, preferential tariffs, weak anti-corruption enforcement, IP protection gaps, ethanol market access, and illegal deforestation. Major exemptions include oil and gas, beef, coffee, oranges, and goods already in transit before July 22 (if entered by July 29). Secretary of State Marco Rubio accused Brazilian President Lula of negotiating in bad faith.

events.title: US Imposes New 10% Section 301 Tariff on Mexico Over Forced-Labor Import Enforcement Gaps
events.detail: The Office of the US Trade Representative announced the results of a Section 301 forced-labor investigation covering 60 economies, imposing new ad valorem tariffs effective July 24–25, 2026. Mexico was placed in the more favorable 10% tier (rather than the 12.5% tier applied to countries with no forced-labor import prohibition at all) because USTR determined it has import bans on the books but has failed to effectively enforce them against goods transiting its supply chains. Crucially, Mexican goods that qualify for duty-free treatment under USMCA rules of origin remain exempt from the new tariff, so the measure primarily affects the roughly 11-16% of Mexico-US trade that does not claim USMCA preference. The action landed in the middle of the ongoing USMCA joint-review negotiations and added a new friction point alongside earlier tariff threats on autos, steel, aluminum, and copper.

events.title: Trump Threatens 30% Reciprocal Tariff on Mexico Starting August 1
events.detail: President Trump announced that reciprocal tariffs on Mexican goods would rise to 30% effective August 1, 2026, escalating pressure during the ongoing USMCA joint review process. The threat came roughly two weeks after the US declined to renew USMCA on its current 16-year terms at the July 1 joint review, and as bilateral negotiating rounds on automotive rules of origin, steel, and aluminum continued. As of mid-July, USMCA-qualifying goods (an estimated 89% of Mexico-US trade) continued to enter under the existing 0% preferential rate, with the 30% threat aimed at non-qualifying goods and intended as leverage ahead of the next negotiating round scheduled for the week of July 20.

events.title: Banxico Holds Benchmark Rate at 6.5% in Unanimous Vote, Signals End of Easing Cycle
events.detail: The Bank of Mexico's governing board unanimously voted to hold its benchmark interest rate at 6.5% at its June 25, 2026 meeting, confirming the two-year easing cycle that began in March 2024 has concluded. Headline inflation continued to ease, falling from 4.45% in April to 3.55% by mid-June, within Banxico's target tolerance range. Policymakers signaled they will likely keep the rate at this level going forward, citing upside risks from trade disruptions tied to the ongoing USMCA review, geopolitical tensions, persistent core inflation, and possible peso depreciation.

events.title: Banxico Cuts Benchmark Rate to 6.5% in Split Vote, Signals End of Two-Year Easing Cycle
events.detail: Mexico's central bank (Banco de México / Banxico) voted 3-2 to cut its benchmark overnight interest rate by 25 basis points to 6.5% — the lowest level since May 2022 — following April inflation data showing a first deceleration since December 2025. The governing board simultaneously signaled this cut marked the end of a two-year-plus easing cycle that had lowered rates from the August 2023 peak of 11.25%. Board members in the minority voted to hold rates, citing continued uncertainty over US tariff impacts on inflation and peso stability. The peso traded at approximately 17.31 per dollar in early May, representing significant strengthening from the 2025 average of approximately 19.20. The rate decision comes against a complex macroeconomic backdrop: while inflation is moderating and the peso has strengthened, Mexico's economy contracted in Q1 2026 (largest decline in over a year) with investment falling 6.6% in 2025. The Banxico decision was interpreted as a signal that monetary policy has done its work and that structural reforms — fiscal stimulus, investment promotion through Plan México Acciones — must now carry the weight of economic revival. The 6.5% rate still provides meaningful real interest rates above the approximately 4% headline inflation reading, preserving Mexico's financial stability credentials.

events.title: Mexico's Labor Poverty Rate Hits Historic Low at 32.3% in Q4 2025, Despite GDP Contraction Warnings
events.detail: Mexico's Labor Ministry (STPS) and CONEVAL released Q4 2025 labor poverty data on May 6, 2026, confirming a historic milestone: the share of Mexicans in households unable to cover basic food needs with wage income fell to 32.3% — the lowest on record since the measure was introduced. Labor Minister Marath Bolaños highlighted the figure as evidence that the minimum wage increases (cumulative 283% since 2018 under AMLO and Sheinbaum) have translated into genuine material gains for low-income workers. Mexico raised the minimum wage again in January 2026 to MX$278.80/day (approximately $16.10/day), the highest nominal level since the modern wage was established. However, the milestone came amid contradictory signals: the Q1 2026 GDP contraction of 0.8% — confirmed by INEGI on April 30 — created downside risk for formal employment in the near term. Bloomberg's May 6 analysis argued that 'Mexico will lose more from a bad USMCA rewrite than from no deal,' noting that the agreement generates approximately $839 billion in annual bilateral trade and sustains millions of formal jobs in manufacturing, agriculture, and services. The labor poverty reduction is credited to formal job creation driven by nearshoring investment — FDI into Mexico's manufacturing sector hit $36.9 billion in 2024, the highest on record — and the sustained minimum wage policy. Critics noted that 32.3% labor poverty still means nearly one in three Mexicans cannot cover basic food needs through labor income alone.

events.title: Mexico's Sovereign Infrastructure Fund (MIP) Seeks to Deploy $12 Billion; World Cup Airspace Security Decree Published
events.detail: Mexico's sovereign infrastructure fund (Fondo Mexicano del Petróleo para la Estabilización y el Desarrollo, MIP) announced it is actively seeking to deploy USD $12 billion in new infrastructure investments — a major complement to the Plan México Acciones framework unveiled the previous day. The deployment targets strategic infrastructure including ports, rail corridors, industrial parks, and energy grid upgrades to support the nearshoring manufacturing boom. Separately, on May 5, Mexico's Secretariat of National Defense (SEDENA) published a formal decree establishing four Zones of Surveillance and Protection of Mexican Airspace (ZVP) for the FIFA World Cup period running from May 11 through July 20, 2026 — covering Mexico City, Guadalajara, and Monterrey. The decree operationalizes Mexico's counter-drone (CUAS) commitments and coordinates military airspace control with civilian aviation authorities. Mexico City's Benito Juárez Airport simultaneously completed three-day tactical exercises simulating hijacking, hostage-taking, and CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear) scenarios. The dual announcements — major investment mobilization and World Cup security finalization — reflected the Sheinbaum government's effort to project institutional capacity despite the Sinaloa governor crisis and US sovereignty disputes of the preceding week.

events.title: Sheinbaum Unveils Plan México Acciones: MX$5.6 Trillion Infrastructure Push to Revive Contracting Economy
events.detail: President Claudia Sheinbaum unveiled 'Plan México Acciones,' an expanded investment framework designed to reverse Mexico's economic contraction after Q1 2026 posted the country's largest GDP decline in over a year. The plan encompasses a MX$5.6 trillion (approximately USD $407 billion) public-private infrastructure investment pipeline for 2026–2030, immediate accelerated tax deductions of 41–91% on new fixed-asset investments, and a unified digital foreign trade platform to reduce bureaucratic friction for exporters. Mexico's sovereign infrastructure fund (MIP) separately announced plans to deploy USD $12 billion in new infrastructure projects. The plan directly responds to a 2025 investment contraction of 6.6% — driven by investor uncertainty over the judicial reform, USMCA tariff tensions, and security concerns. Sheinbaum framed the initiative as Mexico's response to the nearshoring opportunity, with dozens of Asian and US manufacturing companies seeking to relocate supply chains from China to Mexico. The plan attracted cautious interest from the private sector, though business associations noted that judicial certainty and rule-of-law improvements — not tax incentives alone — were the primary investment constraints. Bloomberg noted the initiative came as Mexico sought to project economic confidence ahead of the May 25 USMCA formal review round.

events.title: INEGI Flash Estimate: Mexico's Economy Contracted 0.8% in Q1 2026, All Sectors Declined
events.detail: Mexico's national statistics agency (INEGI) released its flash GDP estimate for Q1 2026 on April 30, showing the economy contracted 0.8% quarter-over-quarter — the worst sequential decline since Q4 2024 and a steeper fall than market consensus. All three major sectors declined: primary activities (agriculture, livestock, fishing) fell 1.4%; industrial activities (manufacturing, construction, mining) fell 1.1%; and tertiary activities (services, commerce, tourism) declined 0.6%. Year-over-year, the economy grew only 0.2% in seasonally adjusted terms, essentially stagnating. The contraction reflected: continued investment uncertainty stemming from the 2024 judicial reform's impact on rule-of-law perceptions; the 25% US tariff on non-USMCA qualifying goods weighing on export-oriented manufacturing; construction delays in major government infrastructure projects; and a deceleration in consumption spending. The data directly prompted Sheinbaum to announce Plan México Acciones four days later (May 4) — a MX$5.6 trillion public-private investment framework intended to reverse the contraction trend. Banxico responded with a 25bp rate cut to 6.5% (May 7). Mexico's full-year 2026 GDP growth forecast was revised down to approximately 1.3%, driven largely by the anticipated World Cup tourism boost in Q2–Q3.

events.title: Sheinbaum Signs Steel Industry Promotion Agreement: All Federal Projects Must Use Mexican Steel
events.detail: President Claudia Sheinbaum signed the 'Acuerdo para el Fomento de la Industria Siderúrgica Nacional' (Agreement for the Promotion of the National Steel Industry) on April 29, 2026, requiring all federal public works projects to use domestically produced steel and iron. The agreement covers 19 federal agencies and three industry chambers — the Cámara Nacional del Acero (Canacero), the Cámara Nacional de la Industria de la Construcción (CNIC), and the Cámara Mexicana de la Industria de la Construcción (CMIC). Anti-Corruption Minister Raquel Buenrostro was designated as the deal's enforcer. Canacero chief Sergio de la Maza called it a 'decisive step' for import substitution, protecting approximately 90,000 direct jobs and providing certainty for over $8 billion in ongoing investment. For 2026, the public sector committed to procuring 150,000 tonnes of reinforcing steel, 150,000 tonnes of structural steel, and over one million tonnes for railway construction. The measure was Sheinbaum's direct economic response after bilateral negotiations to lift US steel and aluminum tariffs failed to reach agreement ahead of the USMCA formal review. By redirecting the government's construction purchasing power — which consumes approximately 60% of Mexico's domestic steel — toward national producers, Mexico essentially launched an import-substitution strategy in the steel sector without a retaliatory tariff. The agreement was unveiled at Wednesday's mañanera alongside the MX$5.6 trillion Plan México Acciones framework announced May 4.
